question.stem: In light reaction, plastoquinone facilitates the transfer of electrons from

steps: In the Z-scheme the electron flow is $\mathrm{PS\text{-}II} \rightarrow \mathrm{PQ} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cyt\,b_{6}f} \rightarrow \mathrm{PC} \rightarrow \mathrm{PS\text{-}I}$, so plastoquinone carries electrons from PS-II to the $\mathrm{Cytb_{6}f}$ complex, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html: 1. In the Z-scheme the electron flow is PS-II → PQ → Cyt b6f → PC → PS-I, so plastoquinone carries electrons from PS-II to the Cytb6f complex, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: In the Z-scheme, plastoquinone is the mobile carrier that takes electrons from PS-II to the cytochrome b6f complex.

(4) When ready-made antibodies are directly given, it is called “Passive immunity”

question.stem: Identify the wrong statement with reference to immunity.

options.text: Active immunity is quick and gives full response

answer.ai_text: Active immunity is quick and gives full response

steps: Active immunity develops when the host's own body produces antibodies after exposure to a living or dead antigen; it is slow and takes time to give its full effective response, so option $1$ is wrong.
Ready-made antibodies given directly, including antibodies passed from mother to foetus through the placenta, give passive immunity, so options $2$, $3$ and $4$ are correct.
The wrong statement is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Active immunity develops when the host's own body produces antibodies after exposure to a living or dead antigen; it is slow and takes time to give its full effective response, so option 1 is wrong.
  2. Ready-made antibodies given directly, including antibodies passed from mother to foetus through the placenta, give passive immunity, so options 2, 3 and 4 are correct.
  3. The wrong statement is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Active immunity is slow and takes time to give its full effective response, so the statement that it is quick is wrong; the other three statements are correct.

question.stem: Match the following concerning essential elements and their functions in plants

steps: Iron is needed for chlorophyll biosynthesis, so $(a) \rightarrow (iii)$.
Zinc is needed for auxin (IAA) synthesis, so $(b) \rightarrow (iv)$.
Manganese takes part in the splitting (photolysis) of water in photosynthesis, so $(d) \rightarrow (i)$.
The remaining item $(c)$ pairs with pollen germination $(ii)$, a boron function.

  2. Zinc is needed for auxin (IAA) synthesis, so (b) → (iv).
  3. Manganese takes part in the splitting (photolysis) of water in photosynthesis, so (d) → (i).
  4. The remaining item (c) pairs with pollen germination (ii), a boron function.
  5. (a)-(iii); (b)-(iv); (c)-(ii); (d)-(i) is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Iron is required for chlorophyll biosynthesis, zinc for IAA (auxin) biosynthesis, Mn for photolysis of water; the remaining (c) (likely boron) fits pollen germination: (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(ii), (d)-(i).

(4) GIFT and ZIFT
question.html:

  3. (3)ZIFT and IUT
  4. (4)GIFT and ZIFT
question.stem: In which of the following techniques, the embryo are transferred to assist those females who cannot conceive?

steps: In ZIFT the zygote or early embryo with up to $8$ blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube, so it is an embryo transfer.
In IUT an embryo with more than $8$ blastomeres is transferred into the uterus, so it is also an embryo transfer.
GIFT transfers an ovum (a gamete), not an embryo, and ICSI injects a sperm directly into the ovum in the laboratory, so neither is an embryo transfer.
Only ZIFT and IUT are embryo-transfer techniques, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In ZIFT the zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube, so it is an embryo transfer.
  2. In IUT an embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus, so it is also an embryo transfer.
  3. GIFT transfers an ovum (a gamete), not an embryo, and ICSI injects a sperm directly into the ovum in the laboratory, so neither is an embryo transfer.
  4. Only ZIFT and IUT are embryo-transfer techniques, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: In ZIFT the zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) is transferred into the fallopian tube, and in IUT an embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus; GIFT transfers gametes and ICSI injects a sperm into the ovum.

question.stem: Match the following columns and select the correct option.

steps: Pituitary gland: deficient ADH from the posterior pituitary causes diabetes insipidus, so $(a) \rightarrow (iii)$.
Thyroid gland: hyperthyroidism (exophthalmic goitre) is Graves' disease, so $(b) \rightarrow (i)$.
Adrenal gland: underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones causes Addison's disease, so $(c) \rightarrow (iv)$.
Pancreas: insulin deficiency from the islets causes diabetes mellitus, so $(d) \rightarrow (ii)$.
The set $(a)-(iii);\ (b)-(i);\ (c)-(iv);\ (d)-(ii)$ is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Pituitary gland: deficient ADH from the posterior pituitary causes diabetes insipidus, so (a) → (iii).
  2. Thyroid gland: hyperthyroidism (exophthalmic goitre) is Graves' disease, so (b) → (i).
  3. Adrenal gland: underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones causes Addison's disease, so (c) → (iv).
  4. Pancreas: insulin deficiency from the islets causes diabetes mellitus, so (d) → (ii).
  5. The set (a)-(iii); (b)-(i); (c)-(iv); (d)-(ii) is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Pituitary (ADH deficiency) - diabetes insipidus; thyroid hyperactivity - Graves' disease; adrenal cortex hypofunction - Addison's disease; pancreas (insulin deficiency) - diabetes mellitus.

Choose the correct pair from the following:

(3) Ligases - Join the two DNA molecules
(4) Polymerases - Break the DNA into fragments
question.html:

  1. (1)Nuclease - Separate the two strange of DNA
  2. (2)Exonuclease - Make cuts at specific positions within DNA
  3. (3)Ligases - Join the two DNA molecules
  4. (4)Polymerases - Break the DNA into fragments
question.stem: Choose the correct pair from the following:

options.text: Nuclease - Separate the two strange of DNA
Exonuclease - Make cuts at specific positions within DNA
Ligases - Join the two DNA molecules
Polymerases - Break the DNA into fragments

answer.ai_text: Ligases - Join the two DNA molecules

steps: Nucleases hydrolyse phosphodiester bonds; they do not separate the two strands of DNA, so option $1$ is wrong.
Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA; cutting at specific positions within DNA is done by endonucleases, so option $2$ is wrong.
DNA polymerases synthesise DNA; they do not break DNA into fragments, so option $4$ is wrong.
DNA ligases join DNA fragments/molecules together, so option $3$ is the correct pair.
ai_solution.html:
1. Nucleases hydrolyse phosphodiester bonds; they do not separate the two strands of DNA, so option 1 is wrong.
  2. Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA; cutting at specific positions within DNA is done by endonucleases, so option 2 is wrong.
  3. DNA polymerases synthesise DNA; they do not break DNA into fragments, so option 4 is wrong.
  4. DNA ligases join DNA fragments/molecules together, so option 3 is the correct pair.
ai_solution.why: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments/molecules; nucleases cut DNA, exonucleases remove terminal nucleotides, polymerases synthesise DNA.

question.stem: The product(s) of reaction catalyzed by nitrogenase in root nodules of leguminous plants is/are:

steps: The nitrogenase reaction is $N_2 + 8e^- + 8H^+ + 16\,ATP \rightarrow 2NH_3 + H_2 + 16\,ADP + 16\,P_i$, so the products are ammonia and hydrogen, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html: 1. The nitrogenase reaction is N2 + 8e- + 8H+ + 16 ATP → 2NH3 + H2 + 16 ADP + 16 Pi, so the products are ammonia and hydrogen, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to NH3 with obligatory evolution of H2: N2 + 8e- + 8H+ + 16ATP -> 2NH3 + H2 + 16ADP + 16Pi.

question.stem: Identify the wrong statement with regard to Restriction Enzymes.

options.text: They are useful in genetic engineering
Sticky ends can be joined by using DNA ligases
Each restriction enzyme functions by inspecting the length of a DNA sequence
They cut the strand of DNA at palindromic sites

answer.ai_text: They cut the strand of DNA at palindromic sites

steps: Option $1$: restriction enzymes are the molecular scissors of genetic engineering, so it is true.
Option $2$: sticky ends formed by restriction enzymes are joined by DNA ligase, so it is true.
Option $3$: NCERT states each restriction endonuclease functions by inspecting the length of a DNA sequence, so it is true.
Option $4$: the enzyme recognises a palindromic sequence but cuts each strand a little away from the centre of the palindrome, so the statement as worded is the wrong one; answer is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Option 1: restriction enzymes are the molecular scissors of genetic engineering, so it is true.
  2. Option 2: sticky ends formed by restriction enzymes are joined by DNA ligase, so it is true.
  3. Option 3: NCERT states each restriction endonuclease functions by inspecting the length of a DNA sequence, so it is true.
  4. Option 4: the enzyme recognises a palindromic sequence but cuts each strand a little away from the centre of the palindrome, so the statement as worded is the wrong one; answer is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Per NCERT, restriction enzymes recognise palindromic sequences but cut a little away from the centre of the palindrome (between the same two bases on opposite strands), so 'cut at palindromic sites' is the intended wrong statement; options 1-3 are NCERT statements.

Which of the following would help in prevention of diuresis?
(1) Atrial natriuretic factor causes vasoconstriction
(2) Decrease in secretion of renin by JG cells
(3) More water reabsorption due to undersecretion of ADH
(4) Reabsorption of $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and water and from renal tubules due to aldosterone
question.html:

  1. (1)Atrial natriuretic factor causes vasoconstriction
  2. (2)Decrease in secretion of renin by JG cells
  3. (3)More water reabsorption due to undersecretion of ADH
  4. (4)Reabsorption of Na+ and water and from renal tubules due to aldosterone
question.stem: Which of the following would help in prevention of diuresis?

options.text: Decrease in secretion of renin by JG cells
More water reabsorption due to undersecretion of ADH
Reabsorption of $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and water and from renal tubules due to aldosterone

answer.ai_text: Reabsorption of $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and water and from renal tubules due to aldosterone

steps: Preventing diuresis means the body must conserve water, so less urine is formed.
Option $1$ is false: ANF causes vasodilation and opposes the RAA mechanism, which promotes diuresis.
Option $2$: less renin from JG cells $\Rightarrow$ less angiotensin II and aldosterone $\Rightarrow$ less $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and water reabsorption, so diuresis increases.
Option $3$ contradicts itself: undersecretion of ADH lowers water reabsorption, which causes diuresis.
Option $4$: aldosterone increases reabsorption of $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and water from the renal tubules, so less urine forms and diuresis is prevented. The answer is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Preventing diuresis means the body must conserve water, so less urine is formed.
  2. Option 1 is false: ANF causes vasodilation and opposes the RAA mechanism, which promotes diuresis.
  3. Option 2: less renin from JG cells ⇒ less angiotensin II and aldosterone ⇒ less Na+ and water reabsorption, so diuresis increases.
  4. Option 3 contradicts itself: undersecretion of ADH lowers water reabsorption, which causes diuresis.
  5. Option 4: aldosterone increases reabsorption of Na+ and water from the renal tubules, so less urine forms and diuresis is prevented. The answer is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Aldosterone increases reabsorption of Na+ and water from the distal parts of the renal tubule, conserving water and so preventing diuresis; the other options are false or would increase diuresis.

question.stem: Which of the following refer to correct example(s) of organisms which have evolved due to changes in environment brought about by anthropogenic action?

Excessive use of herbicides and drugs selects resistant weeds and resistant eukaryotes (and microbes), so $(b)$ and $(c)$ are anthropogenic examples.
Breeds of domesticated animals such as dogs are produced by human (artificial) selection, so $(d)$ is anthropogenic.
Correct set is $(b), (c), (d)$, which is option $1$.

  2. Excessive use of herbicides and drugs selects resistant weeds and resistant eukaryotes (and microbes), so (b) and (c) are anthropogenic examples.
  3. Breeds of domesticated animals such as dogs are produced by human (artificial) selection, so (d) is anthropogenic.
  4. Correct set is (b), (c), (d), which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Herbicide-resistant weeds, drug-resistant eukaryotes and man-made dog breeds all arose from human action; Darwin's finches evolved naturally (adaptive radiation).

question.stem: Identify the substances having glycosidic bond and peptide bond, respectively in their structure:

steps: Inulin is a polysaccharide of fructose units, so its monomers are joined by glycosidic bonds; insulin is a protein (peptide hormone), so its amino acids are joined by peptide bonds.

Lecithin is a phospholipid, cholesterol is a sterol and glycerol is a simple trihydroxy alcohol, so none of these has a peptide or glycosidic bond, which rules out options $1$, $3$ and $4$; the answer is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Inulin is a polysaccharide of fructose units, so its monomers are joined by glycosidic bonds; insulin is a protein (peptide hormone), so its amino acids are joined by peptide bonds.
  2. Lecithin is a phospholipid, cholesterol is a sterol and glycerol is a simple trihydroxy alcohol, so none of these has a peptide or glycosidic bond, which rules out options 1, 3 and 4; the answer is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Inulin is a fructose polysaccharide (glycosidic bonds); insulin is a peptide hormone (peptide bonds).

question.stem: If the distance between two consecutive base pairs is $0.34\,\mathrm{nm}$ and the total number of base pair os a DNA double helix in a typical mammalian cell is $6.6 \times 109\,\mathrm{bp}$, then the length of the DNA is approximately

steps: Length of DNA $L = (\text{number of bp}) \times (\text{distance between consecutive bp})$.
$L = 6.6 \times 10^{9} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}$.
$L = 2.244\,\mathrm{m} \approx 2.2\,\mathrm{m}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Length of DNA L = (number of bp) × (distance between consecutive bp).
  2. L = 6.6 × 109 × 0.34 × 10-9 m.
  3. L = 2.244 m ≈ 2.2 m, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Length = number of bp x distance per bp = 6.6 x 10^9 x 0.34 x 10^-9 m = 2.244 m, approximately 2.2 m.

question.html:

  3. (3)High concentration of Estrogen
  4. (4)High concentration of progesterone
question.stem: Which of the following hormone levels will cause release of ovum (ovulation) from the graafian follicle?

steps: In the follicular phase the growing Graafian follicle secretes more and more estrogen, which reaches a peak just before mid-cycle.
The high estrogen level starts the mid-cycle surge of $LH$ (and $FSH$), and the $LH$ surge causes the Graafian follicle to rupture and release the ovum.
Low $LH$ or low $FSH$ (options $1$ and $2$) is the opposite of what happens, and high progesterone (option $4$) comes from the corpus luteum after ovulation.
This leaves high concentration of estrogen, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In the follicular phase the growing Graafian follicle secretes more and more estrogen, which reaches a peak just before mid-cycle.
  2. The high estrogen level starts the mid-cycle surge of LH (and FSH), and the LH surge causes the Graafian follicle to rupture and release the ovum.
  3. Low LH or low FSH (options 1 and 2) is the opposite of what happens, and high progesterone (option 4) comes from the corpus luteum after ovulation.
  4. This leaves high concentration of estrogen, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: In mid-cycle a high level of estrogen from the growing Graafian follicle sets off the LH surge, which brings about ovulation. LH and FSH are high, not low, at this point, and progesterone rises only after ovulation.

question.stem: The plant parts which consist of two generations one within the other:

statements.label: (b)
statements.text: Germinated pollen grain with two male gametes

steps: (a) Pollen grains are male gametophytes (haploid, $n$) held inside the anther, which is sporophytic tissue ($2n$): two generations, one within the other.
(b) A germinated pollen grain with its two male gametes is all male gametophyte ($n$): one generation only.
(c) A seed (embryo, seed coat) inside a fruit (pericarp) is sporophytic tissue within sporophytic tissue: not gametophyte within sporophyte.
(d) The embryo sac is the female gametophyte ($n$) inside the ovule, which is sporophytic ($2n$): two generations, one within the other.
So (a) and (d) are correct, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. (a) Pollen grains are male gametophytes (haploid, n) held inside the anther, which is sporophytic tissue (2n): two generations, one within the other.
  2. (b) A germinated pollen grain with its two male gametes is all male gametophyte (n): one generation only.
  3. (c) A seed (embryo, seed coat) inside a fruit (pericarp) is sporophytic tissue within sporophytic tissue: not gametophyte within sporophyte.
  4. (d) The embryo sac is the female gametophyte (n) inside the ovule, which is sporophytic (2n): two generations, one within the other.
  5. So (a) and (d) are correct, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Pollen grain (male gametophyte) inside anther and embryo sac (female gametophyte) inside ovule are gametophytic generation within sporophytic tissue; (b) is gametophyte only, (c) is sporophyte tissue around a sporophyte embryo.

solution.html:

  2. V = 14π PPcordr2 = 9 × 104 × 16 × 10-4cos 60(0.6)2

$= \frac{16 \times 9}{36} \times \frac{1}{2} \times 100 = 200V$
For a short dipole, $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p\cos\theta}{r^2}$.
$k p \cos 60^{\circ} = 144 \times 0.5 = 72$.
$V = \frac{72}{0.36} = 200\,\mathrm{V}$, which is option $4$.

question.full_text:
A series LCR circuit is connected to an ac voltage source. When L is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between current and voltage Is $\pi/3$. If instead C is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again $\pi/3$ between current and voltage. The power factor of the circuit is
(1) $1.0$
(2) $-1.0$
(3) Zero
(4) $0.5$
question.html:
A series LCR circuit is connected to an ac voltage source. When L is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between current and voltage Is π/3. If instead C is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again π/3 between current and voltage. The power factor of the circuit is
  1. (1)1.0
  2. (2)-1.0
  3. (3)Zero
  4. (4)0.5
question.stem: A series LCR circuit is connected to an ac voltage source. When L is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between current and voltage Is $\pi/3$. If instead C is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again $\pi/3$ between current and voltage. The power factor of the circuit is

solution.html:
1. tan 60o = Xc12; XL = XC
  2. tan 60o = XL2

steps: With $L$ removed (RC circuit): $\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{X_C}{R}$, so $X_C = \sqrt{3}R$.
With $C$ removed (RL circuit): $\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{X_L}{R}$, so $X_L = \sqrt{3}R$.
Hence $X_L = X_C$, so for the full LCR circuit $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = R$.
Power factor $\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z} = 1$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. With L removed (RC circuit): tanπ3 = XCR, so XC = 3R.
  2. With C removed (RL circuit): tanπ3 = XLR, so XL = 3R.
  3. Hence XL = XC, so for the full LCR circuit Z = R2 + (XL - XC)2 = R.
  4. Power factor cosφ = RZ = 1, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Removing L gives tan(pi/3) = X_C/R and removing C gives tan(pi/3) = X_L/R, so X_L = X_C: the full circuit is at resonance and the power factor is 1.

subtopics.name: Power in an AC Circuit
subtopics.why: Equal phase angles with L removed and with C removed give X_L = X_C, so the LCR circuit is at resonance and its power factor cos(phi) is 1.

step_list: With L removed (RC circuit), write tan(pi/3) = X_C/R
With C removed (RL circuit), write tan(pi/3) = X_L/R, and equate the two to get X_L = X_C
Recognise X_L = X_C as resonance in the full LCR circuit, so Z = R and power factor cos(phi) = R/Z
difficulty.why: The work is writing the phase-angle relation for the RC and RL sub-circuits, equating them to conclude X_L = X_C, then applying the resonance condition to get the power factor of the full circuit.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: One option equals cos(pi/3), the trap for a candidate who takes the given sub-circuit phase angle as the phase of the full LCR circuit.

question.full_text:
Light of frequency $1.5$ times the threshold frequency W incident on a photosensitive material. What will be the photoelectric current if the frequency is halved and intensity is doubled ?
(1) one – fourth
(2) zero
(3) doubled
(4) four times
question.html:
Light of frequency 1.5 times the threshold frequency W incident on a photosensitive material. What will be the photoelectric current if the frequency is halved and intensity is doubled ?
  1. (1)one – fourth
  2. (2)zero
  3. (3)doubled
  4. (4)four times
question.stem: Light of frequency $1.5$ times the threshold frequency W incident on a photosensitive material. What will be the photoelectric current if the frequency is halved and intensity is doubled ?

solution.html: 1. Theoretical
steps: Theoretical

Initial frequency $
u = 1.5\,
u_0$, where $
u_0$ is the threshold frequency.

Halving gives $
u' =  rac{1.5\,
u_0}{2} = 0.75\,
u_0$.
Since $\nu' < \nu_0$, no photoelectrons are emitted, regardless of intensity.
Doubling the intensity does not change this, so the photoelectric current is zero, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Initial frequency ν = 1.5 ν0, where ν0 is the threshold frequency.
  2. Halving gives ν' = 1.5 ν02 = 0.75 ν0.
  3. Since ν' < ν0, no photoelectrons are emitted, regardless of intensity.
  4. Doubling the intensity does not change this, so the photoelectric current is zero, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Halved frequency is 0.75 times the threshold frequency, below threshold, so no photoemission occurs whatever the intensity; current is zero.

step_list: Compute the new frequency: half of 1.5 times the threshold frequency gives 0.75 times the threshold, so it is below threshold
Recall that below the threshold frequency no photoelectrons are emitted whatever the intensity, so the change in intensity has no effect on the current
difficulty.why: One short arithmetic step to compare the new frequency with the threshold, then one recall of the threshold condition for photoemission.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The 'doubled' option is what a candidate gets by applying current proportional to intensity without first checking the frequency against the threshold.

(1) $0.44 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$
(2) $5.00\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$
(3) $0.44 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$
(4) $1.77 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$
question.html:
The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with air as medium is 6 μF. With the introduction of a dielectric medium, the capacitance becomes 30 μF. The permittivity of the medium is : (ε0 = 8.85 × 10-12 C2 N-1 m-2)
  1. (1)0.44 × 10-10 C2 N-1 m-2
  2. (2)5.00 C2 N-1 m-2
  3. (3)0.44 × 10-13 C2 N-1 m-2
  4. (4)1.77 × 10-12 C2 N-1 m-2
question.stem: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with air as medium is $6\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. With the introduction of a dielectric medium, the capacitance becomes $30\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. The permittivity of the medium is : ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$)

solution.html:
1. C = C0 K
  2. 30 = 6 K
  3. K = 5

steps: Dielectric constant $K = \frac{C}{C_0} = \frac{30\,\mu\mathrm{F}}{6\,\mu\mathrm{F}} = 5$.
$\varepsilon = K\varepsilon_0 = 5 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} = 44.25 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$.
$44.25 \times 10^{-12} \approx 0.44 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Dielectric constant K = CC0 = 30 μF6 μF = 5.
  2. ε = Kε0 = 5 × 8.85 × 10-12 = 44.25 × 10-12 C2 N-1 m-2.
  3. 44.25 × 10-12 ≈ 0.44 × 10-10 C2 N-1 m-2, which is option 1.

(1) Semiconductors only
(2) Insulators and semiconductors
(3) Metals
(4) Insulators only

  1. (1)Semiconductors only
  2. (2)Insulators and semiconductors
  3. (3)Metals
  4. (4)Insulators only
question.stem: The solids which have the negative temperature coefficient of resistance are :

solution.html:
1. εm = t0.k
  2. = 5 × 0.05 × 10-12
  3. = 44.25 × 10-12
  4. = 0.44 × 10-10
steps: $\varepsilon_{m} = t_{0}.k$
In metals, rising $T$ increases collisions while $n$ stays fixed, so $\rho$ rises and $\alpha > 0$.
In semiconductors and insulators, rising $T$ excites electrons across the band gap, so $n$ rises sharply and $\rho$ falls, giving $\alpha < 0$.
Both semiconductors and insulators have negative $\alpha$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In metals, rising T increases collisions while n stays fixed, so ρ rises and α > 0.
  2. In semiconductors and insulators, rising T excites electrons across the band gap, so n rises sharply and ρ falls, giving α < 0.
  3. Both semiconductors and insulators have negative α, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Resistivity falls as temperature rises in both semiconductors and insulators (more thermally excited charge carriers), so both have a negative temperature coefficient; metals have a positive one.

For transistor action, which of the following statements is correct?
(1) Both emitter junction as well as the collector junction are forward biased.
(2) The base region must be very thin and lightly doped.
(3) Base, emitter and collector regions should have same doping concentrations
(4) Base, emitter and collector regions should have same size
question.html:
For transistor action, which of the following statements is correct?
  1. (1)Both emitter junction as well as the collector junction are forward biased.
  2. (2)The base region must be very thin and lightly doped.
  3. (3)Base, emitter and collector regions should have same doping concentrations
  4. (4)Base, emitter and collector regions should have same size
question.stem: For transistor action, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Both emitter junction as well as the collector junction are forward biased.
The base region must be very thin and lightly doped.
Base, emitter and collector regions should have same doping concentrations
Base, emitter and collector regions should have same size

answer.ai_text: The base region must be very thin and lightly doped.

solution.html: 1. Semiconductor.
steps: Semiconductor.
In the active mode the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased, so option $1$ is false.
The emitter is heavily doped, the base is lightly doped and the collector is moderately doped, so equal doping (option $3$) is false.
The base is very thin and the collector is the largest region, so equal size (option $4$) is false.
A very thin, lightly doped base lets most carriers injected from the emitter reach the collector, so option $2$ is correct.
ai_solution.html:
1. In the active mode the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased, so option 1 is false.
  2. The emitter is heavily doped, the base is lightly doped and the collector is moderately doped, so equal doping (option 3) is false.
  3. The base is very thin and the collector is the largest region, so equal size (option 4) is false.
  4. A very thin, lightly doped base lets most carriers injected from the emitter reach the collector, so option 2 is correct.
ai_solution.why: For transistor action the base must be very thin and lightly doped so most injected carriers cross to the collector; emitter junction is forward biased and collector junction reverse biased, and regions differ in doping and size.

question.html:
A screw gauge has least count of 0.01 mm and there are 50 divisions in its circular scale. The pitch of the screw guage is
  1. (1)0.5 mm
  2. (2)1.0 mm
  3. (3)0.01 mm
  4. (4)0.25 mm
question.stem: A screw gauge has least count of $0.01\,\mathrm{mm}$ and there are 50 divisions in its circular scale. The pitch of the screw guage is

steps: Least count of a screw gauge: $\mathrm{LC} = \frac{\text{pitch}}{N}$, where $N$ is the number of circular scale divisions.
$\text{pitch} = \mathrm{LC} \times N = 0.01\,\mathrm{mm} \times 50$.
$\text{pitch} = 0.5\,\mathrm{mm}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Least count of a screw gauge: LC = pitchN, where N is the number of circular scale divisions.
  2. pitch = LC × N = 0.01 mm × 50.
  3. pitch = 0.5 mm, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Pitch = least count x number of circular scale divisions = 0.01 mm x 50 = 0.5 mm.

difficulty.why: A single substitution of the given least count and division count into the standard screw-gauge relation LC = pitch / N.

The phase difference between displacement and acceleration of a particle in a simple harmonic motion is :
(1) $\pi/2\,\mathrm{rad}$
(2) zero
(3) $\pi\,\mathrm{rad}$
(4) $3\pi/2\,\mathrm{rad}$
question.html:

  1. (1)π/2 rad
  2. (2)zero
  3. (3)π rad
  4. (4)3π/2 rad
question.stem: The phase difference between displacement and acceleration of a particle in a simple harmonic motion is :

solution.html:
1. α.C = Pitchμ0 of d
  2. 0.01 = Pitchs0 = 0.5m
steps: $\alpha.C = \frac{Pitch}{\mu_0 \text{ of d}}$
Displacement in SHM: $x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$.
Acceleration: $a = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -\omega^2 A\sin(\omega t + \phi) = -\omega^2 x$.
$-\sin\theta = \sin(\theta + \pi)$, so $a = \omega^2 A\sin(\omega t + \phi + \pi)$.
Phase difference between $x$ and $a$ is $\pi\,\mathrm{rad}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Displacement in SHM: x = Asin(ω t + φ).
  2. Acceleration: a = d2xdt2 = -ω2 Asin(ω t + φ) = -ω2 x.
  3. -sinθ = sin(θ + π), so a = ω2 Asin(ω t + φ + π).
  4. Phase difference between x and a is π rad, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: In SHM a = -omega^2 x, so acceleration is always opposite to displacement: phase difference pi rad.

question.stem: A ball is thrown vertically downward with a velocity of $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ from the top of a tower. It hits the ground after some time with a velocity of $80\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The height of the tower is : ($g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)

solution.html:
1. v2 = u2 - 2gh
  2. 64ω = 400 = 29h
  3. 6000 = 20h
  4. h = 300m

steps: Take downward as positive: $u = 20\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $v = 80\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $a = g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Take downward as positive: u = 20 m/s, v = 80 m/s, a = g = 10 m/s2.
  2. Use v2 = u2 + 2gh.
  3. 802 = 202 + 2(10)h ⇒ 6400 = 400 + 20h.
  4. h = 6400 - 40020 = 600020 = 300 m, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Using v^2 = u^2 + 2gh with u = 20 m/s downward, v = 80 m/s, g = 10 m/s^2 gives h = (6400 - 400)/20 = 300 m.

question.html:
The Brewsters angle ib for an interface should be:
  1. (1)450 < ib < 900
  2. (2)ib = 900
  3. (3)00 < ib < 300
  4. (4)300 < ib < 450
question.stem: The Brewsters angle $i_{b}$ for an interface should be:

solution.html:
1. μ = tan θ1
  2. 1 < μ < 90o
  3. 45o < θ < 90o
steps: $\mu = \tan \theta_{1}$
Brewster's law: $\tan i_b = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$.
For light incident from a rarer medium on a denser one (the NCERT case, e.g. air to glass), $\frac{n_2}{n_1} > 1$, so $\tan i_b > 1$ and $i_b > 45^{\circ}$.
$\frac{n_2}{n_1}$ is finite, so $\tan i_b$ is finite and $i_b < 90^{\circ}$.
Hence $45^{\circ} < i_b < 90^{\circ}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Brewster's law: tan ib = n2n1.
  2. For light incident from a rarer medium on a denser one (the NCERT case, e.g. air to glass), n2n1 > 1, so tan ib > 1 and ib > 45°.
  3. n2n1 is finite, so tan ib is finite and ib < 90°.
  4. Hence 45° < ib < 90°, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: tan i_b = n2/n1; for light going from a rarer to a denser medium (e.g. air to glass, as NCERT treats it) n2/n1 > 1, so tan i_b > 1 and 45 deg < i_b < 90 deg.

Apply it to the usual case of light going from a rarer to a denser medium, where n2/n1 > 1, so tan i_b > 1. That puts i_b between 45 and 90 degrees, which picks the matching range from the options

difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The stem does not say that light travels from a rarer to a denser medium; the candidate has to assume it to get tan i_b > 1.

question.stem: A ray is incident at an angle of incidence $i$ on one surface of a small angle prism (with angle of prism $A$) and emerges normally from the opposite surface. If the refractive index of the material of the prism is $\mu$, then the angle of incidence is nearly equal to

solution.html:
1. μ = sin 1osin A
  2. i = μ A
steps: $\mu = \frac{\sin 1^{o}}{\sin A}$
$i = \mu A$

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

unreadable: The figure is a photograph of a rough handwritten pen sketch on paper (a prism with apex angle A, an incident ray at angle i, a dashed normal, and handwritten marks 'A', '90-A', '90°'), not a printed vector drawing; printed_text is empty, so none of its handwritten labels exist in the booklet's text layer and the sketch is not drawn to scale, so its geometry cannot be redrawn without estimating.

steps: The ray emerges normally from the second face, so the angle of refraction there is $r_2 = 0$.
For a prism $r_1 + r_2 = A$, so $r_1 = A$.
Snell's law at the first face: $\sin i = \mu \sin r_1 = \mu \sin A$.
For small angles $\sin i \approx i$ and $\sin A \approx A$, so $i \approx \mu A$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The ray emerges normally from the second face, so the angle of refraction there is r2 = 0.
  2. For a prism r1 + r2 = A, so r1 = A.
  3. Snell's law at the first face: sin i = μ sin r1 = μ sin A.
  4. For small angles sin i ≈ i and sin A ≈ A, so i ≈ μ A, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Normal emergence makes r2 = 0, so r1 = A; Snell's law with small angles gives i = mu A.

subtopics.why: The answer depends on refraction through a thin prism: emergence is normal so r2 = 0, r1 = A, and with small angles i = mu*r1 = mu*A.

step_list: Normal emergence means the angle of refraction at the second face r2 = 0, so from r1 + r2 = A the angle of refraction at the first face is r1 = A
Apply Snell's law at the first face: sin i = mu sin r1 = mu sin A
Use the small-angle approximation sin x ~ x to get i in terms of mu and A
difficulty.why: The work is using the prism-geometry relation r1 + r2 = A with r2 = 0, then Snell's law at the entry face, then the small-angle approximation.

Find the torque about the origin when a force of acts on a particle whose position vector is
(1) $-6\hat{i}\,\mathrm{Nm}$
(2) $6\hat{k}\,\mathrm{Nm}$
(3) $6\hat{i}\,\mathrm{Nm}$
(4) $6\hat{j}\,\mathrm{Nm}$
question.html:
Find the torque about the origin when a force of acts on a particle whose position vector is
  1. (1)-6ˆı Nm
  2. (2)6ˆk Nm
  3. (3)6ˆı Nm
  4. (4)6ˆȷ Nm
question.stem: Find the torque about the origin when a force of acts on a particle whose position vector is

solution.html:
1. →F = 3ˆȷ
  2. →r = 2ˆk
  3. →τ = →r × →F
  4. = 2ˆk × 3ˆȷ
  5. = 6[ˆk × ˆȷ]
  6. = -6ˆȷ
steps: $\vec{F} = 3\hat{j}$
$\vec{r} = 2\hat{k}$
$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$
$= 2\hat{k} \times 3\hat{j}$
$= 6\left[\hat{k} \times \hat{j}\right]$
Torque about the origin is $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$.
The stem gives no vectors; assume $\vec{F} = 3\hat{j}\,\mathrm{N}$ and $\vec{r} = 2\hat{k}\,\mathrm{m}$.
$\vec{\tau} = 2\hat{k} \times 3\hat{j} = 6(\hat{k} \times \hat{j})$.
$\hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}$, so $\vec{\tau} = -6\hat{i}\,\mathrm{Nm}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Torque about the origin is →τ = →r × →F.
  2. The stem gives no vectors; assume →F = 3ˆȷ N and →r = 2ˆk m.
  3. →τ = 2ˆk × 3ˆȷ = 6(ˆk × ˆȷ).
  4. ˆk × ˆȷ = -ˆı, so →τ = -6ˆı Nm, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Stem is missing both vectors; assuming the standard version (F = 3j N, r = 2k m), tau = r x F = 2k x 3j = -6i Nm.

  3. (3)12kBT
  4. (4)32kBT
question.stem: The average thermal energy for a mono-atomic gas is : ($k_B$ is Boltzmann constant and $T$, absolute temperature)

solution.full_text:
1. $U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$
2. $= \frac{f}{2}\frac{N}{N_A}RT$
3. $= \frac{f}{2}N\left(\frac{R}{N_A}\right)^{T}$
4. $U = \frac{f}{2}Nk_{BT}$
5. Where $N \rightarrow$ No. of atoms
6. $\mathrm{N_A} \rightarrow$ Avogadro Number
7. $U \rightarrow$ Total thermal energy

11. Average energy $= U/N$

solution.html:
1. U = f2nRT
  2. = f2NNART
  3. = f2N(RNA)T
  4. U = f2NkBT
  5. Where N → No. of atoms
  6. NA → Avogadro Number
  7. U → Total thermal energy
  8. T → Temperature

steps: $U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$
$= \frac{f}{2}\frac{N}{N_A}RT$
$= \frac{f}{2}N\left(\frac{R}{N_A}\right)^{T}$
$U = \frac{f}{2}Nk_{BT}$
Where $N \rightarrow$ No. of atoms
$\mathrm{N_A} \rightarrow$ Avogadro Number
$U \rightarrow$ Total thermal energy

For mono-atomic gas $f = 3$

A monoatomic gas molecule has only translational motion, so $f = 3$ degrees of freedom.
By the law of equipartition each degree of freedom carries $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$.
$E = 3 \times \frac{1}{2}k_BT = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$, which is option $4$.

steps: Electric energy density: $u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$.

steps: Under forward bias the applied voltage $V$ opposes the built-in potential, so the barrier becomes $V_0 - V$ and the depletion region narrows.
Under reverse bias the applied voltage adds to the built-in potential, so the barrier becomes $V_0 + V$ and the depletion region widens.
So the depletion width increases only under reverse bias, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Under forward bias the applied voltage V opposes the built-in potential, so the barrier becomes V0 - V and the depletion region narrows.
  2. Under reverse bias the applied voltage adds to the built-in potential, so the barrier becomes V0 + V and the depletion region widens.
  3. So the depletion width increases only under reverse bias, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Reverse bias pulls majority carriers away from the junction, uncovering more immobile ions and widening the depletion region; forward bias narrows it.

question.stem: A $40\,\mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor is connected to a $200\,\mathrm{V}$, $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ ac supply. The rms value of the current in the circuit is, nearly :

solution.full_text:
1. $\omega = 2\pi f$
2. $\theta = 2\pi(50)$
3. $= 100\pi\,\mathrm{rad}$
4. Capacitive Reactive $\leftarrow X_c = \frac{1}{\omega c} = \frac{1}{40\times10^{-6}}\times\frac{1}{100\pi}$
5. $= \frac{1}{4\times100^{-3}\times\pi}\,\Omega$
6. $I_{rms} = \frac{V_{rms}}{X_c} = \frac{200}{\frac{1}{4\times10^{-3}\pi}}$
7. $= 200\times4\times10^{-3}\pi$
8. $= 0.8\times\pi$
9. $I_{rms} = 2.51$ Ampere

A series LCR circuit is connected to an ac voltage source. When $L$ is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between current and voltage Is $\pi/3$. If instead $C$ is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again $\pi/3$ between current and voltage. The power factor of the circuit is
(1) $1.0$
(2) $-1.0$
(3) Zero
(4) $0.5$
question.html:
A series LCR circuit is connected to an ac voltage source. When L is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between current and voltage Is π/3. If instead C is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again π/3 between current and voltage. The power factor of the circuit is
  1. (1)1.0
  2. (2)-1.0
  3. (3)Zero
  4. (4)0.5
question.stem: A series LCR circuit is connected to an ac voltage source. When $L$ is removed from the circuit, the phase difference between current and voltage Is $\pi/3$. If instead $C$ is removed from the circuit, the phase difference is again $\pi/3$ between current and voltage. The power factor of the circuit is

solution.html:
1. tan 60o = Xc12; XL = XC
  2. tan 60o = XL2

steps: With $L$ removed (RC circuit): $\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{X_C}{R}$, so $X_C = \sqrt{3}R$.
With $C$ removed (RL circuit): $\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{X_L}{R}$, so $X_L = \sqrt{3}R$.
Hence $X_L = X_C$, so for the full LCR circuit $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = R$.
Power factor $\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z} = 1$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. With L removed (RC circuit): tanπ3 = XCR, so XC = 3R.
  2. With C removed (RL circuit): tanπ3 = XLR, so XL = 3R.
  3. Hence XL = XC, so for the full LCR circuit Z = R2 + (XL - XC)2 = R.
  4. Power factor cosφ = RZ = 1, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Removing L gives tan(pi/3) = X_C/R and removing C gives tan(pi/3) = X_L/R, so X_L = X_C; the full LCR circuit is at resonance and the power factor is 1.

subtopics.name: Power in an AC Circuit
subtopics.why: Equal phase angles with L or C removed give X_L = X_C, so the series LCR circuit is at resonance and its power factor cos(phi) is 1.

step_list: With L removed (RC circuit), write tan(pi/3) = X_C / R
With C removed (RL circuit), write tan(pi/3) = X_L / R, and equate the two to get X_L = X_C
Recognise X_L = X_C as resonance in the full LCR circuit, so the impedance is R and the power factor is cos(phi) = R/Z
difficulty.why: The work is writing the phase-angle relation for each reduced circuit, equating them to get equal reactances, and recognising that equal reactances mean resonance in the full circuit.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Option 0.5 is exactly cos(pi/3), the answer a candidate gets by carrying the given phase angle over to the full circuit instead of combining the two reactances.

  4. (4)four times
question.stem: Light of frequency $1.5$ times the threshold frequency W incident on a photosensitive material. What will be the photoelectric current if the frequency is halved and intensity is doubled ?

solution.html: 1. Theoretical
steps: Theoretical

The incident frequency is $
u = 1.5\,
u_0$, where $
u_0$ is the threshold frequency.

Halving it gives $
u' =  rac{1.5\,
u_0}{2} = 0.75\,

$\nu' < \nu_0$, so no photoelectrons are emitted, whatever the intensity.
Doubling the intensity cannot cause emission below threshold, so the photoelectric current is zero, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The incident frequency is ν = 1.5 ν0, where ν0 is the threshold frequency.
  2. Halving it gives ν' = 1.5 ν02 = 0.75 ν0.

ai_solution.why: Halving 1.5 times the threshold frequency gives 0.75 times the threshold, which is below threshold, so no photoemission occurs whatever the intensity; the current is zero.

step_list: Compute the new frequency relative to threshold: 1.5 times threshold halved gives 0.75 times threshold, i.e. below threshold
Apply the threshold law of the photoelectric effect: below threshold frequency no photoelectrons are emitted whatever the intensity, so the change in intensity is irrelevant

difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The doubled-intensity clause is a distractor: a candidate who applies 'photocurrent is proportional to intensity' without first checking the threshold lands on the 'doubled' option.

question.stem: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with air as medium is $6\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. With the introduction of a dielectric medium, the capacitance becomes $30\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. The permittivity of the medium is : ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$)

solution.html:
1. C = C0 K
  2. 30 = 6 K
  3. K = 5

  3. 44.25 × 10-12 ≈ 0.44 × 10-10 C2 N-1 m-2, which is option 1.

steps: $\varepsilon_{m} = t_{0}.k$
For metals, resistivity rises with temperature, so $\alpha > 0$; this rules out option $3$.
For semiconductors and insulators, the number density $n$ of charge carriers rises with temperature, so $\rho = \frac{m}{n e^2 \tau}$ falls, giving $\alpha < 0$.

  2. (2)ib = 900

question.stem: The Brewsters angle $i_{b}$ for an interface should be:

solution.html:
1. μ = tan θ1
  2. 1 < μ < 90o
  3. 45o < θ < 90o
steps: $\mu = \tan \theta_{1}$
Brewster's law: $\tan i_b = \mu = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$.
For the usual interface (rarer to denser, e.g. air to glass), $\frac{n_2}{n_1} > 1$, so $\tan i_b > 1 = \tan 45^{\circ}$, giving $i_b > 45^{\circ}$.
$\tan i_b$ is finite, so $i_b < 90^{\circ}$; hence $45^{\circ} < i_b < 90^{\circ}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Brewster's law: tan ib = μ = n2n1.
  2. For the usual interface (rarer to denser, e.g. air to glass), n2n1 > 1, so tan ib > 1 = tan 45°, giving ib > 45°.
  3. tan ib is finite, so ib < 90°; hence 45° < ib < 90°, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: tan i_b = n2/n1; for light going from a rarer to a denser medium (e.g. air to glass, n2/n1 > 1), tan i_b > 1 so 45 deg < i_b < 90 deg.

spec.title: A ray refracted at the first face of a small-angle prism of angle A, travelling inside along the normal to the second face

steps: The ray emerges normally from the second face, so the refraction angle there is $r_2 = 0$.
For a prism $r_1 + r_2 = A$, so $r_1 = A$.
Snell's law at the first face: $\sin i = \mu \sin r_1 = \mu \sin A$.
For small angles $\sin i \approx i$ and $\sin A \approx A$, so $i \approx \mu A$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. For a prism r1 + r2 = A, so r1 = A.

  4. For small angles sin i ≈ i and sin A ≈ A, so i ≈ μ A, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Normal emergence gives r2 = 0, so r1 = A; for small angles Snell's law gives i = mu*A.

question.stem: Reaction between benzaldehyde and acetophenone in presence of dilute $\mathrm{NaOH}$ is known as :

steps: Acetophenone ($\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}$) has $\alpha$-hydrogens and forms an enolate in dilute $\mathrm{NaOH}$; benzaldehyde ($\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}$) has none and acts only as the electrophile.
The enolate adds to benzaldehyde and the product dehydrates: $\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO + CH_3COC_6H_5 \xrightarrow{dil.\ NaOH} C_6H_5CH{=}CHCOC_6H_5 + H_2O}$.
Aldol condensation between two different carbonyl compounds is a cross aldol condensation (Claisen-Schmidt), which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Acetophenone (C6H5COCH3) has α-hydrogens and forms an enolate in dilute NaOH; benzaldehyde (C6H5CHO) has none and acts only as the electrophile.
  2. The enolate adds to benzaldehyde and the product dehydrates: C6H5CHO + CH3COC6H5 dil. NaOH  C6H5CH=CHCOC6H5 + H2O.
  3. Aldol condensation between two different carbonyl compounds is a cross aldol condensation (Claisen-Schmidt), which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Two different carbonyl compounds (benzaldehyde with no alpha-H, acetophenone with alpha-H) condense in dilute NaOH: a cross aldol (Claisen-Schmidt) condensation.

The correct option for free expansion of an ideal gas under adiabatic condition is
(1) $q < 0$, $\Delta T = 0$ and $w = 0$
(2) $q > 0$, $\Delta T > 0$ and $w > 0$
(3) $q = 0$, $\Delta T = 0$ and $w = 0$
(4) $q = 0$, $\Delta T < 0$ and $w > 0$
question.html:
The correct option for free expansion of an ideal gas under adiabatic condition is
  1. (1)q < 0, Δ T = 0 and w = 0
  2. (2)q > 0, Δ T > 0 and w > 0
  3. (3)q = 0, Δ T = 0 and w = 0
  4. (4)q = 0, Δ T < 0 and w > 0
question.stem: The correct option for free expansion of an ideal gas under adiabatic condition is

steps: Adiabatic condition: no heat exchange, so $q = 0$.
Free expansion is against $p_{ext} = 0$, so $w = -p_{ext}\Delta V = 0$.
$\Delta U = q + w = 0 + 0 = 0$.
For an ideal gas $U$ depends only on $T$, so $\Delta U = 0 \Rightarrow \Delta T = 0$.
$q = 0$, $\Delta T = 0$, $w = 0$ is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Adiabatic condition: no heat exchange, so q = 0.
  2. Free expansion is against pext = 0, so w = -pextΔ V = 0.
  3. Δ U = q + w = 0 + 0 = 0.
  4. For an ideal gas U depends only on T, so Δ U = 0 ⇒ Δ T = 0.
  5. q = 0, Δ T = 0, w = 0 is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Adiabatic means q = 0; free expansion against zero external pressure gives w = 0; so Delta U = 0 and for an ideal gas Delta T = 0.

step_list: Recall the NCERT statement that free expansion of an ideal gas (into vacuum, adiabatic) has w = 0 because there is no opposing pressure, q = 0 because it is adiabatic, so delta U = 0 and, for an ideal gas, delta T = 0, then pick the option with all three zero

question.stem: Reaction between acetone and methylmagnesium chloride followed by hydrolysis will give

steps: Grignard reagents add to ketones to give tertiary alcohols after hydrolysis.
$(CH_3)_2C{=}O + CH_3MgCl \rightarrow (CH_3)_3C{-}OMgCl$.
$(CH_3)_3C{-}OMgCl \xrightarrow{H_2O} (CH_3)_3C{-}OH + Mg(OH)Cl$, which is tert-butyl alcohol, option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Grignard reagents add to ketones to give tertiary alcohols after hydrolysis.
  2. (CH3)2C=O + CH3MgCl → (CH3)3C-OMgCl.
  3. (CH3)3C-OMgCl H2O  (CH3)3C-OH + Mg(OH)Cl, which is tert-butyl alcohol, option 1.
ai_solution.why: CH3MgCl adds to the carbonyl carbon of acetone (a ketone), giving a tertiary alkoxide that hydrolyses to 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol).

question.full_text:
Which one of the followings has maximum number of atoms
(1) $1\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{O_2(g)}$ [Atomic mass of $\mathrm{O} = 16$]
(2) $1\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{Li(s)}$ [Atomic mass of $\mathrm{Li} = 7$]
(3) $1\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{Ag(s)}$ [Atomic mass of $\mathrm{Ag} = 108$]
(4) $1\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{Mg(s)}$ [Atomic mass of $\mathrm{Mg} = 24$]
question.html:
Which one of the followings has maximum number of atoms
  1. (1)1 g of O2(g) [Atomic mass of O = 16]
  2. (2)1 g of Li(s) [Atomic mass of Li = 7]
  3. (3)1 g of Ag(s) [Atomic mass of Ag = 108]
  4. (4)1 g of Mg(s) [Atomic mass of Mg = 24]
question.stem: Which one of the followings has maximum number of atoms

steps: Number of atoms $\propto$ moles of atoms $= \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}} \times \text{atoms per formula unit}$.
$\mathrm{O_2}$: $\frac{1}{32} \times 2 = \frac{1}{16} \approx 0.0625$ mol atoms.
$\mathrm{Li}$: $\frac{1}{7} \approx 0.143$ mol atoms.
$\mathrm{Ag}$: $\frac{1}{108} \approx 0.0093$ mol atoms.
$\mathrm{Mg}$: $\frac{1}{24} \approx 0.0417$ mol atoms.
$\mathrm{Li}$ has the largest value, so $1\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{Li}$ has the most atoms, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Number of atoms ∝ moles of atoms = massmolar mass × atoms per formula unit.
  2. O2: 132 × 2 = 116 ≈ 0.0625 mol atoms.
  3. Li: 17 ≈ 0.143 mol atoms.
  4. Ag: 1108 ≈ 0.0093 mol atoms.
  5. Mg: 124 ≈ 0.0417 mol atoms.
  6. Li has the largest value, so 1 g of Li has the most atoms, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Moles of atoms in 1 g: O2 = 2/32 = 1/16, Li = 1/7, Ag = 1/108, Mg = 1/24; Li has the largest, so the most atoms.

steps: $n_{\mathrm{N_2}} = \frac{7}{28} = 0.25\,\mathrm{mol}$.
$n_{\mathrm{Ar}} = \frac{8}{40} = 0.20\,\mathrm{mol}$.
$p_{\mathrm{N_2}} = x_{\mathrm{N_2}} \, p_{\text{total}} = \frac{5}{9} \times 27\,\mathrm{bar} = 15\,\mathrm{bar}$, which is option $1$.

  2. nAr = 840 = 0.20 mol.
  3. xN2 = 0.250.25 + 0.20 = 59.
  4. pN2 = xN2   ptotal = 59 × 27 bar = 15 bar, which is option 1.

solution.html:

  2. t = 2.3034.606×10-3log20.2

Identify a molecule which does not exist.
(1) $\mathrm{C_2}$
(2) $\mathrm{O_2}$
(3) $\mathrm{He_2}$
(4) $\mathrm{Li_2}$
question.html:

  2. (2)O2
  3. (3)He2
  4. (4)Li2
question.stem: Identify a molecule which does not exist.

steps: $\mathrm{He_2}$ has $4$ electrons: $\sigma 1s^2\,\sigma^* 1s^2$.
Bond order $= \frac{N_b - N_a}{2} = \frac{2-2}{2} = 0$, so $\mathrm{He_2}$ cannot exist.
$\mathrm{C_2}$: $\frac{8-4}{2} = 2$; $\mathrm{O_2}$: $\frac{10-6}{2} = 2$; $\mathrm{Li_2}$: $\frac{4-2}{2} = 1$; all positive, so they exist.
The molecule that does not exist is $\mathrm{He_2}$, option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. He2 has 4 electrons: σ 1s2 σ* 1s2.
  2. Bond order = Nb - Na2 = 2-22 = 0, so He2 cannot exist.
  3. C2: 8-42 = 2; O2: 10-62 = 2; Li2: 4-22 = 1; all positive, so they exist.
  4. The molecule that does not exist is He2, option 3.
ai_solution.why: He2 has 4 electrons: sigma1s^2 sigma*1s^2, so bond order = (2-2)/2 = 0 and the molecule does not exist; C2, O2 and Li2 all have positive bond orders.

question.stem: Hydrolysis of sucrose is given by the following reaction $\mathrm{Sucrose + H_2O \rightleftharpoons Glucose + Fructose}$ If the equilibrium constant ($K_C$) is $2 \times 10^{13}$ $300\,\mathrm{K}$, teh vale of $\Delta_r G^0$ at the same temperature will be:

steps: Use the relation $\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT \ln K_C$.
Substitute $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $T = 300\,\mathrm{K}$, $K_C = 2 \times 10^{13}$: $\Delta_r G^\circ = -8.314 \times 300 \times \ln(2 \times 10^{13})$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. Substitute R = 8.314 J mol-1 K-1, T = 300 K, KC = 2 × 1013: Δr G° = -8.314 × 300 × ln(2 × 1013), which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Standard Gibbs energy relates to the equilibrium constant by Delta_r G0 = -RT ln K, with K = 2 x 10^13 and T = 300 K.

question.stem: For the reaction, $\mathrm{2Cl(g) \rightarrow Cl_2(g)}$, the correct option is:

steps: Forming the $\mathrm{Cl-Cl}$ bond from two free atoms releases energy, so $\Delta_r H < 0$.
Gas moles change from $2$ to $1$ ($\Delta n_g = -1$), so randomness decreases and $\Delta_r S < 0$.
$\Delta_r H < 0$ and $\Delta_r S < 0$ is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Forming the Cl-Cl bond from two free atoms releases energy, so Δr H < 0.
  2. Gas moles change from 2 to 1 (Δ ng = -1), so randomness decreases and Δr S < 0.
  3. Δr H < 0 and Δr S < 0 is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Bond formation from atoms releases energy (exothermic, ΔH < 0) and 2 mol gas to 1 mol gas lowers disorder (ΔS < 0).

Count gas moles (2 -> 1): fewer gaseous particles means less disorder, so the sign of Delta_r S is negative; then match the pair of signs to an option
difficulty.why: The candidate makes two separate sign judgements: an enthalpy sign from recalling that bond formation is exothermic, and an entropy sign from counting the change in gas moles.

question.full_text:
Find out the solubility of $\mathrm{Ni(OH)_2}$ in $0.1\,\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{NaOH}$ given that the solubility product of $\mathrm{Ni(OH)_2}$ is $2 \times 10^{15}$
(1) $1 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{M}$
(2) $1 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{M}$
(3) $2 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{M}$
(4) $2 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{M}$
question.html:
Find out the solubility of Ni(OH)2 in 0.1 M NaOH given that the solubility product of Ni(OH)2 is 2 × 1015
  1. (1)1 × 10-13 M
  2. (2)1 × 108 M
  3. (3)2 × 10-13 M
  4. (4)2 × 10-8 M
question.stem: Find out the solubility of $\mathrm{Ni(OH)_2}$ in $0.1\,\mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{NaOH}$ given that the solubility product of $\mathrm{Ni(OH)_2}$ is $2 \times 10^{15}$

steps: $\mathrm{Ni(OH)_2 \rightleftharpoons Ni^{2+} + 2OH^-}$, so $K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}][\mathrm{OH^-}]^2 = s(0.1 + 2s)^2$.
Since $s \ll 0.1$, $[\mathrm{OH^-}] \approx 0.1\,\mathrm{M}$ and $K_{sp} \approx s(0.1)^2 = s \times 10^{-2}$.
$s = \frac{2 \times 10^{-15}}{10^{-2}} = 2 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{M}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Ni(OH)2 ⇌ Ni2+ + 2OH-, so Ksp = [Ni2+][OH-]2 = s(0.1 + 2s)2.
  2. Since s ≪ 0.1, [OH-] ≈ 0.1 M and Ksp ≈ s(0.1)2 = s × 10-2.
  3. s = 2 × 10-1510-2 = 2 × 10-13 M, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Common-ion effect: [OH-] = 0.1 M, so s = Ksp/[OH-]^2 = 2x10^-15/0.01 = 2x10^-13 M.

Recognise the common-ion effect: [OH-] = 2s + 0.1, approximated as 0.1 M from NaOH
Solve s = Ksp / (0.1)^2 and match the power of ten to the options
difficulty.why: The work is setting up a Ksp expression for a 1:2 salt with a common ion, making the 2s + 0.1 ~ 0.1 approximation, and doing one division with powers of ten.

question.full_text:
on electrolysis of dil. Sulphuric acid using platinum (Pt) electrode, the product obtained at anode will be:
(1) $\mathrm{H_2S}$ gas
(2) $\mathrm{SO_2}$ gas
(3) Hydrogen gas
(4) Oxygen gas
question.html:
on electrolysis of dil. Sulphuric acid using platinum (Pt) electrode, the product obtained at anode will be:
  1. (1)H2S gas
  2. (2)SO2 gas
  3. (3)Hydrogen gas
  4. (4)Oxygen gas
question.stem: on electrolysis of dil. Sulphuric acid using platinum (Pt) electrode, the product obtained at anode will be:

steps: At the inert $\mathrm{Pt}$ anode the competing oxidations are $2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 4e^-$ ($E^\circ_{ox} = -1.23\,\mathrm{V}$) and $2\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}} + 2e^-$ ($E^\circ_{ox} = -1.96\,\mathrm{V}$).
In dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ the water oxidation is favoured, so $\mathrm{O_2}$ gas is evolved at the anode (hydrogen forms at the cathode), which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. At the inert Pt anode the competing oxidations are 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e- (E°ox = -1.23 V) and 2SO42- → S2O82- + 2e- (E°ox = -1.96 V).
  2. In dilute H2SO4 the water oxidation is favoured, so O2 gas is evolved at the anode (hydrogen forms at the cathode), which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: In dilute H2SO4 water is oxidised at the Pt anode in preference to sulphate ions, so oxygen gas is liberated.

question.full_text:
Which of the following is not correct about carbon monoxide?
(1) The carboxyhemoglobin (haemoglobin bound to $\mathrm{CO}$) is less stable than oxyhaemoglobin.
(2) It is produced due to incomplete combustion.
(3) It forms carboxyhaemoglobin.
(4) It reduces oxygen carrying ability of blood
question.html:
Which of the following is not correct about carbon monoxide?
  1. (1)The carboxyhemoglobin (haemoglobin bound to CO) is less stable than oxyhaemoglobin.
  2. (2)It is produced due to incomplete combustion.
  3. (3)It forms carboxyhaemoglobin.
  4. (4)It reduces oxygen carrying ability of blood
question.stem: Which of the following is not correct about carbon monoxide?

options.text: The carboxyhemoglobin (haemoglobin bound to $\mathrm{CO}$) is less stable than oxyhaemoglobin.
It is produced due to incomplete combustion.
It reduces oxygen carrying ability of blood

answer.ai_text: The carboxyhemoglobin (haemoglobin bound to $\mathrm{CO}$) is less stable than oxyhaemoglobin.

steps: Haemoglobin binds $\mathrm{CO}$ about $200$ times more strongly than $\mathrm{O_2}$, so carboxyhaemoglobin is more stable than oxyhaemoglobin; statement $1$ is false.
Statements $2$, $3$ and $4$ are true: $\mathrm{CO}$ comes from incomplete combustion, forms carboxyhaemoglobin and lowers the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, so the answer is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Haemoglobin binds CO about 200 times more strongly than O2, so carboxyhaemoglobin is more stable than oxyhaemoglobin; statement 1 is false.
  2. Statements 2, 3 and 4 are true: CO comes from incomplete combustion, forms carboxyhaemoglobin and lowers the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, so the answer is option 1.
ai_solution.why: CO binds haemoglobin far more strongly than O2, so carboxyhaemoglobin is more stable than oxyhaemoglobin; statement 1 is false.

This is taught in the air-pollution part of Environmental Chemistry.

question.full_text:
The number of Faradays(F) required to produce $20\mathrm{g}$ of calcium from molten $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ (Atomic mass of Ca = $40\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) is:
(1) 3
(2) 4
(3) 1
(4) 2
question.html:
The number of Faradays(F) required to produce 20g of calcium from molten CaCl2 (Atomic mass of Ca = 40 g mol-1) is:
  1. (1)3
  2. (2)4
  3. (3)1
  4. (4)2
question.stem: The number of Faradays(F) required to produce $20\mathrm{g}$ of calcium from molten $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ (Atomic mass of Ca = $40\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) is:

steps: At the cathode: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Ca}$, so $1$ mol of Ca needs $2\,F$.
$n(\mathrm{Ca}) = \frac{20\,\mathrm{g}}{40\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}} = 0.5\,\mathrm{mol}$.
Charge needed $= 0.5 \times 2\,F = 1\,F$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. At the cathode: Ca2+ + 2e- → Ca, so 1 mol of Ca needs 2 F.
  2. n(Ca) = 20 g40 g mol-1 = 0.5 mol.
  3. Charge needed = 0.5 × 2 F = 1 F, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Ca2+ + 2e- -> Ca needs 2 F per mole; 20 g is 0.5 mol, so 0.5 x 2 = 1 F.

step_list: Convert the given mass of calcium to moles using the atomic mass (20 g / 40 g mol^-1)
Use the cathode half-reaction Ca2+ + 2e- -> Ca (two electrons per Ca) to multiply moles of Ca by the electron count, giving the Faradays needed
difficulty.why: The work is a mass-to-moles conversion followed by applying the 2-electron stoichiometry of Ca2+ reduction (Faraday's law) to get the charge in Faradays.

Elimination reaction of 2-Bromo-pentane to form pent-2-ene is:
(a) $\beta$-Elimination reaction
(b) Follows Zaitsev rule
(c) Dehydration reaction
(d) Dehydration reaction
(1) (b), (c), (d)
(2) (a), (b), (d)
(3) (a), (b), (c)
(4) (a), (c), (d)
question.html:
Elimination reaction of 2-Bromo-pentane to form pent-2-ene is:
  1. (a) β-Elimination reaction
  2. (b) Follows Zaitsev rule
  3. (c) Dehydration reaction
  4. (d) Dehydration reaction
  1. (1)(b), (c), (d)
  2. (2)(a), (b), (d)
  3. (3)(a), (b), (c)
  4. (4)(a), (c), (d)
question.stem: Elimination reaction of 2-Bromo-pentane to form pent-2-ene is:

steps: Removing $\mathrm{H}$ from the $\beta$-carbon and $\mathrm{Br}$ from the $\alpha$-carbon of $\mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_2CH_2CH_3}$ is a $\beta$-elimination, so (a) is true.
The more substituted alkene $\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCH_2CH_3}$ (pent-2-ene) is the major product, as Zaitsev's rule predicts, so (b) is true.
The small molecule lost is $\mathrm{HBr}$, so this is dehydrohalogenation; dehydration (loss of $\mathrm{H_2O}$) is false.
The only option containing (a) and (b) with one other item is option $3$: (a), (b), (c), taking (c) as the dehydrohalogenation statement.
ai_solution.html:
1. Removing H from the β-carbon and Br from the α-carbon of CH3CH(Br)CH2CH2CH3 is a β-elimination, so (a) is true.
  2. The more substituted alkene CH3CH=CHCH2CH3 (pent-2-ene) is the major product, as Zaitsev's rule predicts, so (b) is true.
  3. The small molecule lost is HBr, so this is dehydrohalogenation; dehydration (loss of H2O) is false.
  4. The only option containing (a) and (b) with one other item is option 3: (a), (b), (c), taking (c) as the dehydrohalogenation statement.
ai_solution.why: 2-Bromopentane loses HBr (beta-H and Br) to give the more substituted alkene pent-2-ene: beta-elimination following Zaitsev rule; it is dehydrohalogenation, not dehydration, so (a), (b) and the dehydrohalogenation statement are correct.

question.full_text:
What is change in oxidation number of carbon in the following reaction? $\mathrm{CH_4(g) + 4Cl_2(g) \rightarrow CCl_4(1) + 4HCl(g)}$
(1) $-4$ to $+4$
(2) $0$ to $-4$
(3) $+4$ to $+4$
(4) $0$ to $+4$
question.html:
What is change in oxidation number of carbon in the following reaction? CH4(g) + 4Cl2(g) → CCl4(1) + 4HCl(g)
  1. (1)-4 to +4
  2. (2)0 to -4
  3. (3)+4 to +4
  4. (4)0 to +4
question.stem: What is change in oxidation number of carbon in the following reaction? $\mathrm{CH_4(g) + 4Cl_2(g) \rightarrow CCl_4(1) + 4HCl(g)}$

steps: In $\mathrm{CH_4}$, with H at $+1$: $x + 4(+1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = -4$.
In $\mathrm{CCl_4}$, with Cl at $-1$: $x + 4(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +4$.
So carbon goes from $-4$ to $+4$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In CH4, with H at +1: x + 4(+1) = 0 ⇒ x = -4.
  2. In CCl4, with Cl at -1: x + 4(-1) = 0 ⇒ x = +4.
  3. So carbon goes from -4 to +4, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: In CH4 carbon is -4 (H = +1); in CCl4 carbon is +4 (Cl = -1); so it changes from -4 to +4.

question.full_text:
Which of the following alkane cannot be made in good good yield by wurtz reaction
(1) n-Heptane
(2) n-Butane
(3) n-Hexane
(4) 2,3-dimethylbutane
question.html:
Which of the following alkane cannot be made in good good yield by wurtz reaction
  1. (1)n-Heptane
  2. (2)n-Butane
  3. (3)n-Hexane
  4. (4)2,3-dimethylbutane
question.stem: Which of the following alkane cannot be made in good good yield by wurtz reaction

steps: Wurtz reaction: $2\,R\text{-}X + 2\,Na \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} R\text{-}R + 2\,NaX$, so it gives good yield only of symmetrical alkanes with an even number of carbons.
$n$-Butane $= C_2H_5\text{-}C_2H_5$, from $C_2H_5X$ alone.
$n$-Hexane $= n\text{-}C_3H_7\text{-}n\text{-}C_3H_7$, from $n\text{-}C_3H_7X$ alone.
2,3-Dimethylbutane $= (CH_3)_2CH\text{-}CH(CH_3)_2$, from $(CH_3)_2CHX$ alone.
$n$-Heptane ($C_7$) needs $C_3H_7X + C_4H_9X$, which gives a mixture of $C_6$, $C_7$ and $C_8$ alkanes, so poor yield: option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Wurtz reaction: 2 R-X + 2 Na dry ether  R-R + 2 NaX, so it gives good yield only of symmetrical alkanes with an even number of carbons.
  2. n-Butane = C2H5-C2H5, from C2H5X alone.
  3. n-Hexane = n-C3H7-n-C3H7, from n-C3H7X alone.
  4. 2,3-Dimethylbutane = (CH3)2CH-CH(CH3)2, from (CH3)2CHX alone.
  5. n-Heptane (C7) needs C3H7X + C4H9X, which gives a mixture of C6, C7 and C8 alkanes, so poor yield: option 1.
ai_solution.why: Wurtz coupling gives good yields only of symmetrical alkanes (R-R); n-heptane (C7, odd) would need two different halides (C3 + C4), giving a mixture of alkanes.

answer.ai_text: The oxidation states of chromium in $\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$ are not teh same

steps: In $\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}$: $x + 4(-2) = -2 \Rightarrow x = +6$.
In $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$: $2x + 7(-2) = -2 \Rightarrow x = +6$.
Both are $+6$, so statement B ("not the same") is incorrect.

A (interstitial compounds), C ($\mathrm{Cr^{2+}} \to \mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ gives stable $t_{2g}^3$, stronger reductant than $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$) and D (catalytic activity from variable oxidation states and complex formation) are correct.
Incorrect statement is B, taken as option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In CrO42-: x + 4(-2) = -2 ⇒ x = +6.
  2. In Cr2O72-: 2x + 7(-2) = -2 ⇒ x = +6.
  3. Both are +6, so statement B ("not the same") is incorrect.
  4. A (interstitial compounds), C (Cr2+ → Cr3+ gives stable t2g3, stronger reductant than Fe2+) and D (catalytic activity from variable oxidation states and complex formation) are correct.
  5. Incorrect statement is B, taken as option 2.
ai_solution.why: Cr is +6 in both CrO4^2- and Cr2O7^2-, so statement B (oxidation states not the same) is the incorrect one; A, C and D are correct.

  2. (2)NaCl, MgCl2 and CaCl2
  3. (3)Both CgCl2 and CaCl2
  4. (4)Only NaCl
question.stem: $\mathrm{CHl}$ was passed through a solution of $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ and $\mathrm{NaCl}$. Which of the following compound(s) crystallise(s)?

steps: Passing $\mathrm{HCl}$ gas adds $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions: $\mathrm{HCl \rightarrow H^+ + Cl^-}$, a common ion for all three chlorides.
Crystallisation needs the ionic product to exceed $K_{sp}$; for $\mathrm{NaCl}$, $[\mathrm{Na^+}][\mathrm{Cl^-}] > K_{sp}$ once $[\mathrm{Cl^-}]$ rises, so pure $\mathrm{NaCl}$ crystallises.
$\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ and $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ are far more soluble (deliquescent), so they stay in solution; the answer is only $\mathrm{NaCl}$, option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Passing HCl gas adds Cl- ions: HCl → H+ + Cl-, a common ion for all three chlorides.
  2. Crystallisation needs the ionic product to exceed Ksp; for NaCl, [Na+][Cl-] > Ksp once [Cl-] rises, so pure NaCl crystallises.
  3. CaCl2 and MgCl2 are far more soluble (deliquescent), so they stay in solution; the answer is only NaCl, option 4.
ai_solution.why: Common ion effect: HCl raises [Cl-], so the ionic product exceeds Ksp only for the least soluble chloride, NaCl; the highly soluble CaCl2 and MgCl2 stay in solution.

question.full_text:
An increase in the concentration of the reactants of a reaction leads to change in:
(1) Threshold energy
(2) Collision frequency
(3) Activation energy
(4) Heat of reaction
question.html:
An increase in the concentration of the reactants of a reaction leads to change in:
  1. (1)Threshold energy
  2. (2)Collision frequency
  3. (3)Activation energy
  4. (4)Heat of reaction
question.stem: An increase in the concentration of the reactants of a reaction leads to change in:

steps: By collision theory, $\text{rate} = Z_{AB}\, e^{-E_a/RT}$, and the collision frequency $Z_{AB}$ depends on how many reactant molecules are in unit volume.
Raising the concentration raises the number of molecules in unit volume, so $Z_{AB}$ increases.
Threshold energy, $E_a$ and $\Delta H$ depend on the nature of the reaction (and on a catalyst), not on concentration, so they do not change. The answer is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. By collision theory, rate = ZAB  e-Ea/RT, and the collision frequency ZAB depends on how many reactant molecules are in unit volume.
  2. Raising the concentration raises the number of molecules in unit volume, so ZAB increases.
  3. Threshold energy, Ea and Δ H depend on the nature of the reaction (and on a catalyst), not on concentration, so they do not change. The answer is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Raising reactant concentration puts more molecules in unit volume, so they collide more often; threshold energy, activation energy and heat of reaction do not change.

question.full_text:
The calculated spin only magnetic moment of $\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}$ ion is:
(1) $5.92\,\mathrm{BM}$
(2) $2.84\,\mathrm{BM}$
(3) $3.87\,\mathrm{BM}$
(4) $4.90\,\mathrm{BM}$
question.html:
The calculated spin only magnetic moment of Cr2+ ion is:
  1. (1)5.92 BM
  2. (2)2.84 BM
  3. (3)3.87 BM
  4. (4)4.90 BM
question.stem: The calculated spin only magnetic moment of $\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}$ ion is:

steps: Cr ($Z=24$) is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1$, so $\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}$ is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^4$.
A $3d^4$ ion has $n = 4$ unpaired electrons.
$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24}\,\mathrm{BM}$.
$\sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\,\mathrm{BM}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Cr (Z=24) is [Ar] 3d5 4s1, so Cr2+ is [Ar] 3d4.
  2. A 3d4 ion has n = 4 unpaired electrons.
  3. μ = n(n+2) = 4 × 6 = 24 BM.
  4. 24 ≈ 4.90 BM, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Cr2+ is 3d4 with 4 unpaired electrons, so spin-only moment = sqrt(4(4+2)) = sqrt(24) = 4.90 BM.

steps: Positive deviation from Raoult's law occurs when $A$-$B$ interactions are weaker than $A$-$A$ and $B$-$B$ interactions, so $\Delta_{mix}H > 0$ and $p > p_{Raoult}$.
Acetone + chloroform forms a hydrogen bond between $\mathrm{CHCl_3}$ and the carbonyl oxygen, so it shows negative deviation (option $1$ ruled out).
Chloroethane + bromoethane and benzene + toluene are similar molecules and form nearly ideal solutions (options $2$ and $4$ ruled out).
In ethanol + acetone, acetone molecules come between ethanol molecules and break their hydrogen bonds, weakening interactions, so the mixture shows positive deviation, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Positive deviation from Raoult's law occurs when A-B interactions are weaker than A-A and B-B interactions, so ΔmixH > 0 and p > pRaoult.
  2. Acetone + chloroform forms a hydrogen bond between CHCl3 and the carbonyl oxygen, so it shows negative deviation (option 1 ruled out).
  3. Chloroethane + bromoethane and benzene + toluene are similar molecules and form nearly ideal solutions (options 2 and 4 ruled out).
  4. In ethanol + acetone, acetone molecules come between ethanol molecules and break their hydrogen bonds, weakening interactions, so the mixture shows positive deviation, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Acetone breaks the hydrogen bonds between ethanol molecules, so A-B interactions are weaker than A-A/B-B, giving positive deviation; acetone+chloroform is negative, the other two are nearly ideal.

question.stem: Urea reacts with water to form A which will decompose to form B. B when passed through $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ (aq), deep blue colour solution C is formed. What is the formula of C from the following?

steps: Urea is hydrolysed: $\mathrm{NH_2CONH_2 + H_2O \rightarrow NH_2COONH_4}$, so A is ammonium carbamate.
A decomposes: $\mathrm{NH_2COONH_4 \rightarrow 2NH_3 + CO_2}$, so B is $\mathrm{NH_3}$.
$\mathrm{NH_3}$ with $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$(aq) forms the deep blue complex: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 4NH_3 \rightarrow [Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}}$.
So C is $\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Urea is hydrolysed: NH2CONH2 + H2O → NH2COONH4, so A is ammonium carbamate.
  2. A decomposes: NH2COONH4 → 2NH3 + CO2, so B is NH3.
  3. NH3 with Cu2+(aq) forms the deep blue complex: Cu2+ + 4NH3 → [Cu(NH3)4]2+.
  4. So C is [Cu(NH3)4]2+, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Urea hydrolyses to ammonium carbamate (A), which decomposes to NH3 (B); NH3 with Cu2+(aq) gives the deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex [Cu(NH3)4]2+ (C).

question.html:

question.stem: The freezing point depression constant ($K_f$) af benzene is $5.12\,\mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$. The freezing points depression for the solution of molality $0.087\,\mathrm{n}$ containing a non-electrolyte solute in benzene is (rounded off upto two decimal places):

steps: For a non-electrolyte ($i = 1$), $\Delta T_f = K_f \, m$.
$\Delta T_f = 5.12\,\mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}} \times 0.087\,\mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}} = 0.4454\,\mathrm{K} \approx 0.45\,\mathrm{K}$.
No option equals $0.45\,\mathrm{K}$; the nearest is $0.40\,\mathrm{K}$, which is option $1$.
With $m = 0.078$ instead: $5.12 \times 0.078 = 0.3994 \approx 0.40\,\mathrm{K}$, exactly option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For a non-electrolyte (i = 1), Δ Tf = Kf   m.
  2. Δ Tf = 5.12 K kg mol-1 × 0.087 mol kg-1 = 0.4454 K ≈ 0.45 K.
  3. No option equals 0.45 K; the nearest is 0.40 K, which is option 1.
  4. With m = 0.078 instead: 5.12 × 0.078 = 0.3994 ≈ 0.40 K, exactly option 1.
ai_solution.why: Delta Tf = Kf x m = 5.12 x 0.087 = 0.445 K, which matches no option exactly; 0.40 K is the closest, and a molality of 0.078 would give exactly 0.40 K.

question.stem: which of the following oxoacid of solphur has - O - O - linkage?

steps: $\mathrm{H_2S_2O_8}$ (peroxodisulphuric acid) is $\mathrm{HO_3S{-}O{-}O{-}SO_3H}$: the two $\mathrm{SO_3H}$ units are joined by a peroxide $-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}-$ bridge.
$\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}$ (pyrosulphuric acid) is $\mathrm{HO_3S{-}O{-}SO_3H}$: a single $\mathrm{S{-}O{-}S}$ bridge, no $\mathrm{O{-}O}$ bond.
$\mathrm{H_2SO_3}$ and $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ each have one S atom bonded only to $=\mathrm{O}$ and $-\mathrm{OH}$ groups, so no $\mathrm{O{-}O}$ bond.
Only $\mathrm{H_2S_2O_8}$ has the $-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}-$ linkage, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. H2S2O8 (peroxodisulphuric acid) is HO3S-O-O-SO3H: the two SO3H units are joined by a peroxide -O-O- bridge.
  2. H2S2O7 (pyrosulphuric acid) is HO3S-O-SO3H: a single S-O-S bridge, no O-O bond.
  3. H2SO3 and H2SO4 each have one S atom bonded only to =O and -OH groups, so no O-O bond.
  4. Only H2S2O8 has the -O-O- linkage, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Peroxodisulphuric acid H2S2O8 has the structure HO3S-O-O-SO3H, containing a peroxide -O-O- linkage; the others have no O-O bond.

options.text: Vapour phase refining is carried out for Nickel by Van Arkel method.

answer.ai_text: Pig iron can be moulded into a variety of shapes.

steps: Option 1 is false: vapour phase refining of nickel is the Mond process ($\mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}$); the van Arkel method refines Zr/Ti via iodides.
Option 2 is true: pig iron (about $4\%$ C) from the blast furnace can be moulded into a variety of shapes.
Option 3 is false: wrought (malleable) iron is the purest commercial iron; iron with about $4\%$ C is pig iron.
Option 4 is false: blister copper's blistered look is due to evolution of $\mathrm{SO_2}$, not $\mathrm{CO_2}$.
So the correct statement is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Option 1 is false: vapour phase refining of nickel is the Mond process (Ni(CO)4); the van Arkel method refines Zr/Ti via iodides.
  2. Option 2 is true: pig iron (about 4% C) from the blast furnace can be moulded into a variety of shapes.
  3. Option 3 is false: wrought (malleable) iron is the purest commercial iron; iron with about 4% C is pig iron.
  4. Option 4 is false: blister copper's blistered look is due to evolution of SO2, not CO2.
  5. So the correct statement is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Pig iron from the blast furnace (about 4% C) can be cast into a variety of shapes; Ni vapour refining is Mond process, wrought iron is the purest commercial iron, and blister copper's blisters come from SO2.

(1) prop-2-en-1-ylcyclohexane [SMILES: C=CCC1CCCCC1]
(2) propylcyclohexane [SMILES: CCCC1CCCCC1]
(3) prop-1-en-1-ylcyclohexane [SMILES: CC=CC1CCCCC1]
(4) 3-propylcyclohex-1-ene [SMILES: CCCC1C=CCCC1]

steps: Ozonolysis cleaves $C=C$ into two carbonyls; methanal $HCHO$ forms only from a terminal $=CH_2$ carbon.
Option 1: $C_6H_{11}-CH_2-CH=CH_2 \xrightarrow{O_3,\ Zn/H_2O} C_6H_{11}-CH_2-CHO + HCHO$, so methanal forms.
Option 2 ($C_6H_{11}CH_2CH_2CH_3$) is an alkane with no $C=C$, so no ozonolysis.
Option 3 ($C_6H_{11}-CH=CH-CH_3$) gives $C_6H_{11}CHO + CH_3CHO$, no methanal.
Option 4 (ring $C=C$ in 3-propylcyclohexene) gives a single open-chain dialdehyde, no methanal.
Only option $1$ gives methanal.
ai_solution.html:
1. Ozonolysis cleaves C=C into two carbonyls; methanal HCHO forms only from a terminal =CH2 carbon.
  2. Option 1: C6H11-CH2-CH=CH2 O3, Zn/H2O  C6H11-CH2-CHO + HCHO, so methanal forms.
  3. Option 2 (C6H11CH2CH2CH3) is an alkane with no C=C, so no ozonolysis.
  4. Option 3 (C6H11-CH=CH-CH3) gives C6H11CHO + CH3CHO, no methanal.
  5. Option 4 (ring C=C in 3-propylcyclohexene) gives a single open-chain dialdehyde, no methanal.
  6. Only option 1 gives methanal.
ai_solution.why: Methanal (HCHO) comes only from a terminal =CH2 group; option 1 (allylcyclohexane, CH2-CH=CH2) is the only structure with one.

question.full_text:
Which of the following set of molecules will have zero dipole moment?
(1) Nitrogen trifluoride, beryllium difluoride, water, 1, 3-dichlorobenzene
(2) Boron trifluoride, beryllium difluoride, carbon dioxide, 1, 4-dichlorobenzene
(3) Ammonia, beryllium difluoride, water, 1, 4-dichlorobenzene
(4) Boron trifluoride, hydrogen fluoride, carbon dioxide, 1, 3-dichlorobenzene

steps: $\mathrm{BF_3}$ is trigonal planar ($sp^2$), so the three $\mathrm{B-F}$ bond dipoles at $120^\circ$ cancel: $\mu = 0$.
$\mathrm{BeF_2}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ are linear, so their two equal bond dipoles point opposite and cancel: $\mu = 0$.
In 1,4-dichlorobenzene the two $\mathrm{C-Cl}$ dipoles are at $180^\circ$ and cancel: $\mu = 0$.
$\mathrm{NF_3}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$ (pyramidal), $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (bent), $\mathrm{HF}$ and 1,3-dichlorobenzene ($120^\circ$ between dipoles) all have $\mu \neq 0$, ruling out options $1$, $3$ and $4$.
Only option $2$ has all four molecules with $\mu = 0$.
ai_solution.html:
1. BF3 is trigonal planar (sp2), so the three B-F bond dipoles at 120° cancel: μ = 0.
  2. BeF2 and CO2 are linear, so their two equal bond dipoles point opposite and cancel: μ = 0.
  3. In 1,4-dichlorobenzene the two C-Cl dipoles are at 180° and cancel: μ = 0.
  4. NF3, NH3 (pyramidal), H2O (bent), HF and 1,3-dichlorobenzene (120° between dipoles) all have μ ≠ 0, ruling out options 1, 3 and 4.
  5. Only option 2 has all four molecules with μ = 0.
ai_solution.why: BF3 (trigonal planar), BeF2 (linear), CO2 (linear) and 1,4-dichlorobenzene (para, opposite C-Cl dipoles) all have bond dipoles that cancel, giving zero net dipole moment.

step_list: Recall or derive the shape of each small molecule listed (NF3/NH3 pyramidal, H2O bent, HF diatomic, BeF2 and CO2 linear, BF3 trigonal planar)
Apply bond-dipole vector cancellation to the substituted benzenes: para-dichloro dipoles cancel, meta-dichloro dipoles do not
Eliminate each option that contains at least one polar molecule and keep the set in which every member has zero net dipole
difficulty.why: The work is recalling the geometry of about eight molecules and applying dipole-vector cancellation to each, including the meta/para isomer distinction on the benzene ring, then eliminating options by finding the polar member.
